offence_severity: Minimum 6 years, Maximum 7 years rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: The deceased and her child died by drowning
number_of_offences: Charged under Section 304-B IPC; upheld by High Court
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimony of PW-1 and PW-3 regarding dowry harassment, and the evidence of PW-5 that he saw the deceased weeping at the PCO on 16.02.2001. The Court also considered the post-mortem report indicating the probable time of death.
witness_credibility: The Court stated that the credibility of witnesses as assessed by the lower courts is not ordinarily reappraised by this Court, and the findings of the trial court and High Court were accepted as final unless vitiated by errors of law or procedure.

legal_representation.accused: Dr. J.P. Dhanda, Ms. Raj Rani Dhanda, Vineet Dhanda, N.A. Usmani, K.P. Singh, Gopi Chand, Advs.
legal_representation.state: Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Manadakini Singh, Advs.

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Section 304-B IPC, reduced sentence from 8 years to 7 years
appeal_history.high_court: Affirmed conviction under Section 304-B IPC, reduced sentence from 8 years to 7 years

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that there was material in the form of testimony of PW-1 and PW-3 regarding dowry harassment, and that the law enjoins under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act drawing of the presumption that the accused has committed dowry death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the Court did not consider the evidence given by the appellant and that neither cruelty nor any demand for dowry is made out, with the deceased wife apparently taking her life along with her daughter due to being taunted by PW3.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in an appeal under Article 136, the Court will not reassess the evidence at large, particularly when it has been concurrently accepted by the High Court and the Courts below, and that the Court will not interfere unless there is a violation of principles of natural justice, error of law or procedure, misreading of evidence, or the conclusion of the High Court is manifestly perverse and unsupportable.
precedent_relied_upon: Saravanabhavan and Govindaswamy v. State of Madras AIR 1966 SC 1273; Mst. Dalbir Kaur and Others v. State of Punjab (1976) 4 SCC 158; Sushil Ansal v. State Through Central Bureau of Investigation (2014) 6 SCC 173; Major Singh and Another v. State of Punjab (2015) 5 SCC 201; Rajinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2015) 6 SCC 477; G.V. Siddaramesh v. State of Karnataka (2010) 3 SCC 152; Ashok Kumar v. State of Haryana (2010) 12 SCC 350
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the trial court's and high court's findings that the accused had committed dowry death under Section 304-B of the IPC, and that the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act was not rebutted.
